payload.text:
Lighthouses are painted in stripes so that a ship can tell which lighthouse it is looking at. Many coastlines have several lights within sight of each other, and a mariner who sees a flash at night needs to match it to a specific tower on the chart. A distinctive daytime pattern does the same job when visibility is good: a red-and-white spiral, a black-and-white band, or a bold horizontal stripe can be identified from miles away with a glass.

The stripes also make the structure easier to see. Plain white towers can vanish against a bright sky, snow, or surf, and a dark stone tower can blend into cliffs. High-contrast bands break up the outline and give the eye an edge to pick out, even when the light is poor or the tower is far off.

The colours were chosen for practical reasons as well. Red and white were common because the paints were cheap, durable against salt air, and easy to repaint on a regular schedule. Maintenance crews could renew the pattern with a few coats of the same materials, and any change in the scheme would be obvious to sailors who knew the old one.

Some of the best-known examples are in Europe and North America. Cape Hatteras, Bodie Island, and several Scottish and Breton lights all use bands or spirals. Mariners used these patterns for generations, and many lights still keep them today.
